corpus_role: #1 baseline — candidate name appears in header only, never in prose
extraction_notes: Text layer extracted cleanly apart from page-number fusion: '1EDUCATION' and a trailing bare '2'.
'improving user experience by 30' — the '%' is lost in extraction. Harmless here but shows the text layer is lossy.
Field paths are unverified against the deconstructor. locator_mode is 'document' until reconciled; then re-pin to 'field'.

spans.subject: candidate
spans.note: ALL CAPS. spaCy NER degrades noticeably on fully-capitalised names — casing is a feature it relies on. If tier 0 (structural field lookup) fails and this falls through to NER, expect a miss. Good early signal for whether the header is being caught structurally or by luck.

spans.subject: candidate
spans.note: Longest-match: contains jd-003's string. Must be resolved before counting LOCATION occurrences.

spans.subject: candidate
spans.note: Canonical US format. Should be a tier-1 regex certainty.

spans.subject: candidate
spans.note: NO SCHEME. A URL regex anchored on 'https?://' misses this completely. Very common in resumes — people paste the display form. Test explicitly.

spans.subject: candidate
spans.note: Also schemeless. Note 'GitHub' appears separately in the SKILLS list as a technology — see negative_controls. Same token, different meaning, one is PII-adjacent and one is not.

spans.subject: candidate
spans.note: Inside jd-005. The candidate's name, minus the space, lowercased. Neither NER nor a name-string tokenizer will match it against 'JOHN DOE'. Only caught as a side effect of suppressing the whole URL. This is the argument for suppressing URL fields wholesale rather than scanning their contents.

spans.subject: candidate
spans.note: Email local part. Recovers the full name including the word boundary.

spans.subject: candidate
spans.note: Occurrence 2 of 4 in document order; occurrence 1 is nested inside jd-002 and must be consumed by longest-match first. This one sits in the WORK EXPERIENCE line for ABC Company.

spans.subject: candidate
spans.note: EDUCATION line. Note the preceding text is '1EDUCATION' — a fused page number. If the deconstructor section-splits on the literal 'EDUCATION' header it may fail here, orphaning this line into the wrong section. Worth watching independently of the PII question.

spans.subject: candidate
spans.note: NER may classify this as ORG or as LOCATION depending on context words. If it lands as LOCATION it will be tokenized in phase 1 — a false positive that degrades the education section of the output. Watch for it.

negative_controls.note: Product name. Also a common English adjective — high false-positive risk.
Two capitalised words, no context cue. Classic NER false ORG/PERSON.
Reads as a given name — 'Junit' is one character from 'Juniit'/'Junito'. Genuine PERSON risk.
Appears in SKILLS as a technology, distinct from jd-006's URL. Must not be suppressed there or the skills section loses content.

negative_controls.value: Oracle Certified Professional, Java SE 8 Programmer
negative_controls.note: Certification title. Contains 'Oracle' (ORG) and looks credential-ish.
Also an Indonesian island — LOCATION false-positive risk. If tokenized, every skills mention becomes ⟪LOC_n⟫ and the resume is destroyed. Highest-value negative control in this document.

known_traps: ALL-CAPS name (jd-001) — tests whether the header is caught structurally or is quietly relying on NER.
Schemeless URLs (jd-005, jd-006) — the single most likely tier-1 regex gap.
Name derivatives in three separate places (jd-007/008/009) — invisible to both NER and string-match tokenization.
'Java' as a negative control — a LOCATION false positive here would be catastrophic and obvious, which makes it a good canary for over-tokenization.
Nested LOCATION inside ADDRESS — tests the harness's longest-match-first overlap rule, not the detector.
